claim: Oscillations arise in many real-world systems and are associated with both functional and dysfunctional states.
source: Oscillations arise in many real-world systems and are associated with both functional and dysfunctional states.
evidence: This is a general statement about oscillations in real-world systems, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: An odd number of inhibitory nodes and strong enough connections are necessary to generate oscillations in a single cycle threshold-linear network.
source: Here, we provide a proof that uses dynamical system theory to prove that an odd number of inhibitory nodes and strong enough connections are necessary to generate oscillations in a single cycle threshold-linear network.
evidence: This claim is proven analytically in the manuscript using dynamical system theory (Theorem 2).

claim: Oscillations in the brain take part in information transfer.
source: In the brain for instance, oscillations take part in information transfer Fries, 2015; Hahn et al., 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Persistent beta band (13-30 Hz) oscillations are associated with the pathological symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: However, persistent beta band (13-30 Hz) oscillations are associated with the pathological symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) Brown et al., 2001.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2001.

claim: The Poincaré–Bendixson theorem is only valid in two dimensions.
source: The main tool that can be used is the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem Poincaré, 1880; Bendixson, 1901 which is only valid in two dimensions, which drastically reduces its applicability.
evidence: This is a well-known property of the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem, supported by citations.

claim: In most physical, chemical, and biological networks, it is usually not possible to get the correct value of connectivity strength.
source: For example, in most physical, chemical, and biological networks, it is usually not possible to get the correct value of connectivity strength.
evidence: This is a general observation about the practical limitations in measuring network parameters.

claim: It is much easier to know whether two nodes in a system are physically connected and what is the sign (positive or negative) of their interactions than to measure connectivity strength.
source: By contrast, it is much easier to know whether two nodes in a system are physically connected and what is the sign (positive or negative) of their interactions.
evidence: This is a practical observation about experimental feasibility.

claim: Thomas conjectured that the assumption on the constant sign of the Jacobian matrix may not be necessary, and having a negative loop in some domain of the phase space should be sufficient to generate oscillations.
source: Thomas also conjectured that the assumption on the constant sign of the Jacobian matrix may not be necessary Thomas, 2006, that is having a negative loop in some domain of the phase space should be sufficient to generate oscillations.
evidence: This is a statement of Thomas' second conjecture, supported by a citation.

claim: Oscillations can emerge from a simple two populations, excitatory and inhibitory (EI), network Wilson-Cowan model.
source: For instance, oscillations can emerge from a simple two populations, excitatory and inhibitory (EI), network Wilson-Cowan model (Ledoux and Brunel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ledoux and Brunel, 2011.

claim: When connections are too weak, a single cycle threshold-linear network cannot oscillate as the system possesses a unique globally asymptotically stable fixed point, regardless of the sign of the loop.
source: We show analytically that regardless of the sign of this loop, the system cannot oscillate when connections are too weak as the system possesses a unique globally asymptotically stable fixed point.
evidence: This is proven analytically in the manuscript (Theorem 2).

claim: When connections are strong enough in a single cycle threshold-linear network, the system either possesses two asymptotically stable fixed points (positive loop) or a unique unstable fixed point (negative loop).
source: However, when connections are strong enough (see Theorem 2), the system either possesses two asymptotically stable fixed points (positive loop) or a unique unstable fixed point (negative loop).
evidence: This is proven analytically in the manuscript (Theorem 2).

claim: When a single cycle threshold-linear network has strong enough connections and an odd number of inhibitory nodes, the system can have one of the following long term behaviors: limit cycle, quasi-periodic or chaotic behavior.
source: In addition, the system can be shown to be bounded and thus, it has one of the following long term behavior: limit cycle, quasi-periodic or chaotic behavior.
evidence: This is proven analytically in the manuscript (Theorem 2).

claim: Oscillations in a single cycle threshold-linear network can be shut down by introducing a positive external input to excited nodes.
source: Interestingly, we can show that such dynamics can be shut down by introducing a positive external input to excited nodes.
evidence: This is proven analytically in the manuscript (Remark 3).

claim: The subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus (STN-GPe) subnetwork is traditionally considered to be the key network underlying the emergence of oscillations in Parkinson's disease.
source: Traditionally, the subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus (STN-GPe) subnetwork is considered to be the key network underlying the emergence of oscillations in PD (Plenz and Kitai, 1996; Terman et al., 2002; Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent experiments have shown that near complete inhibition of GPe but not of STN is sufficient to quench oscillations in Parkinson's disease.
source: However, recent experiments have shown that near complete inhibition of GPe but not of STN is sufficient to quench oscillations (Crompe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crompe et al., 2020.

claim: There are at least six possible cycles in the Cortex-BG network that have the potential to drive oscillations based on the connectivity structure.
source: Our theory suggests that there are at least six possible cycles in the Cortex-BG network that have the potential to drive oscillations based on the connectivity structure.
evidence: This is derived from the analytical results and network structure analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: GPe is involved in five out of six oscillatory cycles in the Cortex-BG network.
source: Interestingly, we found that GPe is involved in five out of six oscillatory cycles and therefore GPe inhibition is likely to affect PD-related oscillations in most cases.
evidence: This is derived from the network structure analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A network of two mutually connected excitatory populations will not oscillate but will synchronize.
source: If we connect them mutually with excitatory synapses, intuitively we can say that the two-population network will not oscillate. Instead, the two populations will synchronize.
evidence: This is an intuitive explanation based on network dynamics principles.

claim: A network of two mutually connected inhibitory populations cannot oscillate; one node will emerge as a winner and the other will be suppressed.
source: If both these nodes are inhibitory, one of the nodes will emerge as a winner and the other will be suppressed Ermentrout, 1992. Hence, a network of two mutually connected inhibitory populations cannot oscillate either.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ermentrout, 1992.

claim: A three population network with three excitatory connections forming a closed loop will synchronize and cannot oscillate.
source: When all three connections in the cycle are excitatory, the three populations will synchronize. Essentially, we will have a single population. Thus, these two and three population motifs are not capable of oscillations.
evidence: This is an intuitive explanation based on network dynamics principles.

claim: The simplest network motif capable of oscillating consists of two mutually connected nodes: one excitatory and one inhibitory (EI motif).
source: The simplest network motif which is capable of oscillating thus consists of two mutually connected nodes: one excitatory and one inhibitory (EI motif: Figure 1a, bottom; Ledoux and Brunel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: A three population cycle with one inhibitory connection (EEI motif) can be effectively reduced to an EI motif and can therefore oscillate.
source: A cycle with one inhibitory connection (EEI motif) can be effectively reduced to an EI motif and can therefore oscillate.
evidence: This is an inference based on network dynamics principles.

claim: A three population cycle with two inhibitory connections (EII motif) cannot oscillate because the two inhibitory neurons engage in winner-take-all type dynamics.
source: However, when there are two inhibitory connections (EII motif, Figure 1a, top), the two inhibitory neurons engage in a winner-take-all type dynamics and the network is not capable of oscillations.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1a and explained based on network dynamics principles.

claim: A three population cycle with three inhibitory connections (III motif) can exhibit oscillations through winner-less-competition.
source: Finally, if there are three inhibitory connections (i.e. all three nodes are inhibitory, III motif) the network enters in a winner-less-competition Rabinovich et al., 2001 and can exhibit oscillations (Figure 1a, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: A network can generate oscillations if there are one or three inhibitory connections in the network.
source: These examples of two or three nodes suggest that a network can generate oscillations if there are one or three inhibitory connections in the network.
evidence: This is a generalization based on the examples provided in the manuscript.

claim: A possible condition for a one cycle TLN to oscillate is that the number of inhibitory nodes is odd when the connection strengths are strong enough.
source: Then, Theorem 2 says that a possible condition for the one cycle TLN to oscillate is that the number of inhibitory nodes is odd when the connection strength are strong enough (i.e. Equation 5 and Equation 7).
evidence: This is a direct consequence of Theorem 2.

claim: When a TLN network has an odd number of inhibitory nodes and strong enough connections, the system has no stable fixed point and has one of limit cycle, quasi-periodic or chaotic behaviors.
source: In that case, the system has no stable fixed point and from Lemma 1 it is bounded so it has one of limit cycle, quasi-periodic or chaotic behaviors.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of Theorem 2 and Lemma 1.

claim: For a wide range of parameters (synaptic delays, synaptic weights, external input and self-inhibition), the III network showed oscillations while the EII network only resulted in transient oscillations in Wilson-Cowan model simulations.
source: Our numerical simulation showed that for a wide range of parameters (synaptic delays, synaptic weights, external input and self-inhibition), while III network showed oscillations, EII network only resulted in transient oscillations (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerical simulations shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: Increasing the synaptic delay reduced the oscillation frequency in Wilson-Cowan model simulations.
source: For instance, increasing the synaptic delay reduced the oscillation frequency (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Synaptic delays play a more important role in shaping the oscillations in an EI type network.
source: Synaptic delays play a more important role in shaping the oscillations in an EI type network (see Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In networks with even number of inhibitory connections (e.g. EII, EEE, II), synaptic delays are the sole mechanism for initiating oscillations, but unless delays are precisely tuned such oscillations will remain transient.
source: In networks with even number of inhibitory connections (e.g. EII, EEE, II), synaptic delays are the sole mechanism for initiating oscillations, however, unless delays are precisely tuned such oscillations will remain be transient (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of increasing the synaptic strength on oscillation frequency was contingent on the external inputs in Wilson-Cowan model simulations.
source: The effect of increasing the synaptic strength was contingent on the external inputs. In general, increasing the synaptic strength resulted in a reduction in the oscillation frequency (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Oscillation frequency changed in a non-monotonic fashion as a function of external input in Wilson-Cowan model simulations.
source: Next, oscillation frequency changed in a non-monotonic fashion as a function of external input irrespective of the choice of other parameters (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: A mid-range input strength resulted in maximum oscillation frequency in Wilson-Cowan model simulations.
source: Typically, a mid-range input strength resulted in maximum oscillation frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: Increasing the self-connection of nodes increased the oscillation frequency but beyond a certain self-connection the node was completely silenced and oscillations disappeared in Wilson-Cowan model simulations.
source: Finally, increasing the self-connection of nodes increased the oscillation frequency but beyond a certain self-connection the node was completely silenced and it changed the network topology and oscillations disappeared (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Emergence of 15–30 Hz (beta band) oscillations in the cortico-basal ganglia (CBG) network is an ubiquitous feature of Parkinson's disease.
source: Emergence of 15–30  Hz (beta band) oscillations in the cortico-basal ganglia (CBG) network is an ubiquitous feature of PD Raz et al., 2000; Bergman et al., 1998; Sharott et al., 2014; Neumann et al., 2016.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The STN-GPe subnetwork has emerged as the most likely generator of beta oscillations in Parkinson's disease based on connectivity and activity.
source: Based on their connectivity and activity subthalamic nucleus (STN) and the globus pallidus externa (GPe) subnetwork has emerged as the most likely generator of beta oscillations Plenz and Kital, 1999; Bevan et al., 2002.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The STN-GPe subnetwork becomes oscillatory when their mutual connectivity is altered.
source: The STN-GPe subnetwork becomes oscillatory when their mutual connectivity is altered Terman et al., 2002; Holgado et al., 2010 or neurons become bursty Tachibana et al., 2011; Bahuguna et al., 2020 or striatal inputs to GPe increase Kumar et al., 2011; Mirzaei et al., 2017; Sharott et al., 2017; Chakravarty et al., 2022.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Oscillations in the basal ganglia might be generated by the striatum.
source: However, oscillations might also be generated by the striatum McCarthy et al., 2011, by the interaction between the direct and hyperdirect pathways Leblois et al., 2006 and even by cortical networks that project to the BG (Brittain and Brown, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Crompe et al., 2020 showed that GPe is essential to generate beta band oscillations while motor cortex and STN are not.
source: Recently, Crompe et al., 2020 used optogenetic manipulations to shed light on the mechanisms underlying oscillation generation in PD. They showed that GPe is essential to generate beta band oscillations while motor cortex and STN are not.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crompe et al., 2020.

claim: The CBG network can be partitioned into 246 subnetworks with 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7 nodes.
source: The CBG network can be partitioned into 246 subnetworks with 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7 nodes (see Figure 4—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is derived from the network structure analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are five loops (or cycles) in the CBG network with one or three inhibitory projections: Proto-STN, STN-GPi-Th-cortex, STN-Arky-D2-Proto, Proto-Arky-D2, Proto-FSN-D2, and Proto-GPi-Th-Cortex-D2.
source: Among these partitions, there are five loops (or cycles) in the CBG network with one or three inhibitory projections: Proto-STN, STN-GPi-Th-cortex, STN-Arky-D2-Proto, Proto-Arky-D2, Proto-FSN-D2, and Proto-GPi-Th-Cortex-D2 (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is derived from the network structure analysis and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: One or more of the six oscillatory loops appeared in 96 (out of 246) subnetworks of CBG.
source: One or more of these 6 loops appeared in 96 (out of 246) subnetworks of CBG (see Figure 4b, colors indicate different loops).
evidence: This is derived from the network structure analysis and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In Wilson-Cowan model simulations of a four-node BG motif, for weak inputs to the D2-SPNs, the Proto-STN subnetwork generated oscillations for weak positive input.
source: We found that for weak inputs to the D2-SPNs, the Proto-STN subnetwork generated oscillations for weak positive input (Figure 4c bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4c.

claim: As the input to D2-SPNs increased in Wilson-Cowan model simulations, the oscillation frequency decreased and oscillations were observed even for very strong drive to STN.
source: However, as the input to D2-SPNs increased, the oscillation frequency decreased and oscillations were observed even for very strong drive to STN (Figure 4c bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4c.

claim: In Wilson-Cowan model simulations, both Proto-STN and Proto-D2-Arky subnetworks compete for oscillations, with the winner depending on their inputs.
source: That is, in this model, both Proto-STN and Proto-D2-Arky subnetworks compete for oscillations, which subnetwork wins depending on their inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: When D2-SPN to Proto projections were removed in Wilson-Cowan model simulations, the network could oscillate but only because of the Proto-STN subnetwork.
source: When we removed the D2-SPN to Proto projections, the network could oscillate but only because of the Proto-STN subnetwork (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4d.

claim: In Wilson-Cowan model simulations with D2-SPN to Proto projections removed, relatively high-frequency beta band oscillations were observed but only for a small range of excitatory inputs to the STN.
source: In this setting, we get relatively high-frequency beta band oscillations but only for a small range of excitatory inputs to the STN (Figure 4d, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4d.

claim: When STN output was removed in Wilson-Cowan model simulations, the Proto-D2-Arky subnetwork generated oscillations for weak positive inputs to the D2-SPNs.
source: Next, we removed the STN output (equivalent to inhibition of STN), the Proto-D2-Arky subnetwork generated oscillations for weak positive inputs to the D2-SPNs (Figure 4e, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The frequency of Proto-D2-Arky oscillations was smaller than that observed for the Proto-STN subnetwork because the former involves a three synapses loop.
source: The frequency of Proto-D2-Arky oscillations was smaller than that observed for the Proto-STN subnetwork because the former involves a three synapses loop.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the network structure.

claim: It is possible for CBG network to oscillate even when STN is removed from the network.
source: Overall, these results suggest that, in principle, it is possible for CBG network to oscillate even when STN is removed from the network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: In the Proto-D2-FSN loop, D2-SPN neurons have a relatively high firing rate, which could be a criterion to exclude this loop as a potential contributor to beta oscillations.
source: In the loop Proto-D2-FSN, D2-SPN neurons have a relatively high firing rate. This could be a criterion to exclude this loop as a potential contributor to the beta oscillations.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results and a speculation about its implications.

claim: In spiking neuron model simulations with Proto-D2-Arky loop generating oscillations, as STN neurons were inhibited, firing rate of Proto neurons decreased and oscillations in STN population diminished but Proto neurons showed clear beta band oscillations.
source: In the Proto-D2-Arky mode, as we inhibited STN neurons, firing rate of the Proto neurons decreased and oscillations in STN population diminished but Proto neurons showed clear beta band oscillations (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In spiking neuron model simulations with STN-Proto loop generating oscillations, increasing the STN inhibition abolished the oscillations in both STN and Proto neurons.
source: By contrast, and as expected when STN-Proto loop was generating the oscillations, increasing the STN inhibition abolished the oscillations in both STN and Proto neurons (Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In STN-Proto loop, when STN is inhibited, there is no cycle left in the network and therefore oscillations diminished, whereas the Proto-D2-Arky loop remains unaffected by the STN inhibition (except for a change in the firing rate of the Proto neurons).
source: In STN-Proto loop, when STN is inhibited, there is no cycle left in the network and therefore oscillations diminished, whereas the Proto-D2-Arky loop remains unaffected by the STN inhibition (except for a change in the firing rate of the Proto neurons).
evidence: This is an explanation of the simulation results based on network structure.

claim: Whether oscillations are generated by the Proto-D2-Arky or STN-Proto loop depends on the relative input to the D2 or STN neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 4c, whether oscillations are generated by the Proto-D2-Arky or STN-Proto loop depends on the relative input to the D2 or STN neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 4c.

claim: It is possible that in rodents, D2-SPN have stronger input from the cortex than STN and therefore, oscillations survive despite near complete inhibition of STN.
source: So it is possible that in rodents, D2-SPN have stronger input from the cortex than STN and therefore, oscillations survive despite near complete inhibition of STN.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the simulation results and experimental observations.

claim: Together with previous results of Snoussi, 1998 and Gouzé, 1998, this work further expands the scope within which we can comment on the potential of a network to generate oscillation based only on the connectivity structure alone.
source: Thus, together with previous results of Snoussi, 1998 and Gouzé, 1998 we further expand the scope within which we can comment on the potential of a network to generate oscillation based only on the connectivity structure alone.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the work in relation to previous research.

claim: The weights' strength needs to be strong enough for a system to possibly oscillate.
source: In addition, we complete this condition by one on weights' strength stating that the latter needs to be strong enough for the system to possibly oscillate.
evidence: This is a key finding from the analytical results (Theorem 2).

claim: Oscillations can be quenched by adding positive external input to excited nodes.
source: Eventually, oscillations can be quenched by adding positive external input to excited nodes.
evidence: This is a key finding from the analytical results (Remark 3).

claim: A key assumption of the analysis is that there are no delays in the network.
source: A key assumption of our analysis is that there are no delays in the network.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions of the analytical work.

claim: Delays within and between subnetwork connections can have a big effect on the oscillations.
source: Indeed, delays within and between subnetwork connections can have a big effect on the oscillations Kim et al., 2020.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: In numerical simulations of BG network with biologically realistic synaptic delays, such delays do not influence the results and they only determine the oscillation frequency.
source: In the numerical simulations of BG network, we included biologically realistic synaptic delays (i.e. connection delays were shorter than the time constants of the neurons). Our results suggest that such delays do not influence our results and they only determine the oscillation frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: It is not possible to comment on how the results may change when delays become longer than the time constant of the node.
source: But it is not possible to comment on how the results may change when delays become longer than the time constant of the node.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current work.

claim: Previous models suggest that when we excite the excitatory node or inhibit the inhibitory node oscillations can emerge and strengthen.
source: Previous models suggest that when we excite the excitatory node or inhibit the inhibitory node oscillations can emerge and strengthen Kumar et al., 2011; Ledoux and Brunel, 2011.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When we inhibit the excitatory node or excite the inhibitory node, oscillations are quenched.
source: By contrast, when we inhibit the excitatory node or excite the inhibitory node, oscillations are quenched.
evidence: This is a statement based on previous models and general understanding.

claim: The 'Oscillations Sign Rule' states that if we multiply the sign of the node and sign of the stimulation, we can comment on the fate of oscillations in a qualitative manner.
source: This can be summarised as the 'Oscillations Sign Rule'. Let us label the excitatory population as positive and inhibitory as negative. Let us also label excitatory inputs as positive and inhibitory inputs as negative. Now if we multiple the sign of the node and sign of the stimulation, we can comment on the fate of oscillations in a qualitative manner.
evidence: This is a conceptual framework proposed in the manuscript.

claim: The 'Oscillation sign rule' scales to larger network with more nodes.
source: The 'Oscillation sign rule' scales to larger network with more nodes.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the proposed rule.

claim: When we combine the 'Oscillations Sign Rule' with the 'Odd Cycle Rule' we can get a more complete qualitative picture of whether stimulating a node in a network will generate oscillations or not.
source: When we combine the 'Oscillations Sign Rule' with the 'Odd Cycle Rule' we can get a more complete qualitative picture of whether a stimulating a node in a network will generate oscillations or not.
evidence: This is a statement about the combined utility of the two rules.

claim: Biological properties such as spike frequency adaptation, rebound spiking, short-term-facilitation or short-term-depression can be absorbed in the network structure in the form of an extra inhibitory or excitatory connection.
source: For instance, biological neurons have the property of spike frequency adaptation or rebound spiking. Similarly, synapses in the brain can increase or decrease their weights based on the recent history of inputs which is referred to as the short-term-facilitation or short-term-depression of synapses Stevens and Wang, 1995. Such biological properties can be absorbed in the network structure in the form of an extra inhibitory or excitatory connection.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about how biological properties can be represented in network models, with a citation for synaptic properties.

claim: From 2-node-motifs to 6-node-motifs in the basal ganglia, the odd cycle rule identified 88 potential directed cycles that can generate oscillations.
source: From 2-node-motifs to 6-node-motifs, our odd cycle rule identified 88 potential directed cycles that can generate oscillations.
evidence: This is derived from the network structure analysis of the basal ganglia.

claim: Among the 88 potential oscillatory cycles in the basal ganglia, 81 cycles feature GPe (either Proto or Arky type or both) and 66 feature STN.
source: Among these, 81 cycles feature GPe (either Proto or Arky type or both) and 66 feature STN.
evidence: This is derived from the network structure analysis of the basal ganglia.

claim: Which specific cycle underlies oscillations in the basal ganglia depends on the exact input structure.
source: Which specific cycle underlies oscillations depends on the exact input structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: When input to STN is higher than the D2 neurons, the STN-GPe network generates oscillations.
source: For instance, when input to STN is higher than the D2 neurons, the STN-GPe network generates oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: When inputs to D2 neurons are stronger, the D2-Proto-Arky cycle can become the oscillator.
source: But when inputs to D2 neurons are stronger, the D2-Proto-Arky cycle can become the oscillator.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: STN is not necessary to generate oscillations in the basal ganglia.
source: That is, STN is not necessary to generate oscillations in the BG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analytical and simulation results.

claim: Besides focusing on the network connectivity, we should also estimate the inputs to different nodes in order to pinpoint the key nodes underlying the PD-related pathological oscillations.
source: Our results also suggest that besides focusing on the network connectivity, we should also estimate the inputs to different nodes in order to pinpoint the key nodes underlying the PD-related pathological oscillations - that would be the way to reconcile the recent findings of Crompe et al., 2020 with previous results.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the manuscript.

claim: Ortone et al., 2023 and Azizpour Lindi et al., 2023 have provided a more quantitative explanation of the experimental observation by Crompe et al., 2020.
source: We would like to note that recently, Ortone et al., 2023 and Azizpour Lindi et al., 2023 have provided a more quantitative explanation of the experimental observation by Crompe et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a statement about recent related work, supported by citations.

claim: Ortone et al., 2023 and Azizpour Lindi et al., 2023 eventually resort to the D2-Proto-Arky cycle to explain BG oscillations in the absence of STN.
source: They also eventually resort to the D2-Proto-Arky cycle to explain BG oscillations in the absence of STN.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusions of recent related work.

claim: The work provides the necessary theory to explain the results of Ortone et al., 2023 and Azizpour Lindi et al., 2023.
source: Our work provides the necessary theory to explain their results.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the current work in relation to recent research.

claim: Oscillatory dynamics and the odd cycle rule show up in many chemical, biological and even social systems such as neuronal networks, psychological networks, social and political networks, resting-state networks in autism and gene networks.
source: However, oscillatory dynamics and the odd cycle rule show up in many chemical, biological and even social systems such as neuronal networks Bel et al., 2021, psychological networks Greenwald et al., 2002, social and political networks Leskovec et al., 2010; Milo et al., 2004; Heider, 1946; Cartwright and Harary, 1956, resting-state networks in autism Moradimanesh et al., 2021 and gene networks Farcot and Gouzé, 2010; Allahyari et al., 2022.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to various fields.

claim: Originally Thomas' conjecture about the structural conditions for oscillations was made for gene regulatory networks.
source: In fact, originally Thomas' conjecture Thomas, 1980 about the structural conditions for oscillations was made for gene regulatory networks.
evidence: This is a historical statement about Thomas' conjecture, supported by a citation.

claim: Insights obtained from the analytical work can be extended to many other chemical, biological and social networks.
source: Therefore, we think that insights obtained from our analytical work can be extended to many other chemical, biological and social networks.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.
